about: Transfer Processes 1 (CENG40004) is a 7.5-credit core Year 1 module on Imperial's MEng Chemical Engineering, running across the Autumn and Spring terms. No official Imperial module descriptor was found. A third-party UC Education Abroad Program (UCEAP) course listing (last reviewed 2024-25) describes it as covering fluids at rest and in motion (incompressible flow, flow measurement and pipe flow) and the basics of heat and mass transfer by conduction, diffusion and convection, taught from first principles. The breakdown into topics and their order are this pack's own, built from that description; an older, undated UCEAP listing also mentions simple one-dimensional compressible flow, which is not covered here. No module-level assessment breakdown was found on official pages.
topics: Conservation of mass and the Bernoulli equation
Pipe flow: laminar and turbulent friction and pumping
Convective mass transfer and heat–mass transfer analogies

notes.body:
A fluid deforms continuously under any shear stress, however small. Liquids and gases are both fluids; the main practical difference is that liquids are nearly incompressible while gas density depends strongly on pressure and temperature.

Key properties (typical values near 20 °C, approximate)
- Density ρ (kg/m³): water ≈ 1000, air at 1 atm ≈ 1.2, mercury ≈ 13 600.
- Dynamic viscosity μ (Pa s): water ≈ 1.0 × 10⁻³, air ≈ 1.8 × 10⁻⁵.
- Kinematic viscosity ν = μ/ρ (m²/s): water ≈ 1.0 × 10⁻⁶, air ≈ 1.5 × 10⁻⁵.
Viscosity of liquids falls as temperature rises; viscosity of gases rises with temperature.

Newton's law of viscosity
For a Newtonian fluid in simple shear, τ = μ du/dy: shear stress is proportional to the velocity gradient. Water, air and most simple liquids are Newtonian. Non-Newtonian fluids (polymer solutions, slurries, blood, paints) have an apparent viscosity that depends on shear rate: shear-thinning fluids become less viscous when sheared faster, while a Bingham plastic needs a yield stress before it flows at all.

Hydrostatics
In a fluid at rest, pressure changes only with depth: dP/dz = −ρg (z measured upwards). For a liquid of constant density:
P = P_surface + ρgh,
where h is depth below the surface. Pressure at a point acts equally in all directions, and points at the same level in the same continuous fluid have the same pressure.

Worked example: depth and layered liquids
- 10 m of water: ρgh = 1000 × 9.81 × 10 = 98.1 kPa gauge, about one atmosphere.
- A tank holds 2 m of oil (ρ = 850 kg/m³) floating on 3 m of water. At the bottom: P_gauge = 850 × 9.81 × 2 + 1000 × 9.81 × 3 = 16.7 + 29.4 = 46.1 kPa (147.4 kPa absolute with 101.3 kPa atmosphere).

Manometers
- Piezometer and U-tube manometers convert a pressure difference into a liquid height.
- For a U-tube containing manometer fluid of density ρ_m beneath a process fluid of density ρ, a reading h gives ΔP = (ρ_m − ρ)gh.
- Example: mercury under water, h = 0.2 m: ΔP = (13 600 − 1000) × 9.81 × 0.2 = 24.7 kPa.
- Forgetting to subtract the process fluid density is a classic error when the process fluid is a liquid; for a gas, ρ is negligible compared with ρ_m.

Buoyancy and forces on surfaces
- Archimedes' principle: the upward force on an immersed body equals the weight of fluid displaced, F_B = ρ_fluid g V_displaced.
- The force on a plane submerged surface equals the pressure at its centroid times its area; for a vertical or inclined surface it acts at the centre of pressure, below the centroid.

Pressure units
Absolute pressure = gauge + atmospheric. 1 bar = 10⁵ Pa; 1 atm = 101 325 Pa; pressure head h = P/(ρg).

Exam tips: work from a known pressure through the fluid level by level, adding ρgh going down and subtracting going up; state whether answers are gauge or absolute.

notes.h: Conservation of mass and the Bernoulli equation
notes.body:
Continuity
At steady state the mass flow through a stream tube or pipe is constant: ρ₁A₁u₁ = ρ₂A₂u₂. For an incompressible fluid this becomes Q = A₁u₁ = A₂u₂, where u is the mean velocity. Halving a pipe diameter quarters the area, so the velocity rises by a factor of four.

The Bernoulli equation
For steady, incompressible, inviscid (frictionless) flow along a streamline, with no shaft work or heat transfer:
P/ρ + u²/2 + gz = constant (energy per unit mass, J/kg)
or in head form, dividing by g:
P/(ρg) + u²/(2g) + z = constant (metres).
The three terms are pressure head, velocity head and elevation head. Where a fluid speeds up, its pressure falls.

Worked example: contraction
Water (ρ = 1000 kg/m³) flows at 2 m/s in a 100 mm pipe that narrows to 50 mm, horizontally.
- u₂ = 2 × (100/50)² = 8 m/s.
- P₁ − P₂ = ½ρ(u₂² − u₁²) = 0.5 × 1000 × (64 − 4) = 30 kPa.
- Q = (π/4)(0.1)² × 2 = 0.0157 m³/s.

Worked example: draining tank (Torricelli)
For a large open tank with a small hole at depth h below the surface, surface and jet are both at atmospheric pressure and the surface velocity is negligible, so u = √(2gh). For h = 2 m, u = 6.26 m/s. A real jet is slower and narrower, which is handled with a discharge coefficient.

Extending Bernoulli: the mechanical energy balance
Real flows have friction and may include pumps. Between points 1 and 2:
P₁/(ρg) + u₁²/(2g) + z₁ + h_pump = P₂/(ρg) + u₂²/(2g) + z₂ + h_f
where h_pump is the head added by a pump and h_f the frictional head loss. The pump power delivered to the fluid is ρgQh_pump, and the shaft power is this divided by the pump efficiency. This is the steady-flow energy equation with the thermal terms set aside: friction converts mechanical energy into internal energy, which is why h_f is a "loss".

Assumptions to state
- Steady flow; incompressible (fine for liquids, and for gases if pressure changes are small, roughly when the Mach number is below about 0.3).
- Points on the same streamline (or in irrotational flow).
- No friction, unless h_f is included.
- For mean velocities in pipes, a kinetic energy correction factor α appears in front of u²/2: about 2 for fully developed laminar flow and close to 1 for turbulent flow, so α = 1 is usual for turbulent problems.

Exam tips: pick points where you know most quantities (free surfaces at atmospheric pressure, jets discharging to atmosphere), use continuity to link velocities, and keep all pressures either gauge or absolute.

Most industrial flowmeters taught in a first course use Bernoulli and continuity: create a known change in velocity and measure the pressure change it causes.

Venturi meter
A smooth converging section, a throat and a gradual diverging section. Applying Bernoulli between the upstream section (1) and the throat (2), with continuity u₁ = u₂(A₂/A₁):
u₂ = √[2ΔP / (ρ(1 − β⁴))], where β = d₂/d₁
Q = C_d A₂ u₂
- The discharge coefficient C_d corrects for friction and non-uniform velocity; for a well-made venturi it is typically about 0.95–0.99 (approximate).
- Most of the pressure drop is recovered in the diverging section, so the permanent loss is small.

Worked example: venturi
d₁ = 100 mm, d₂ = 50 mm (β = 0.5, β⁴ = 0.0625), water, ΔP = 20 kPa, C_d = 0.98.
- u₂ = √[2 × 20 000/(1000 × 0.9375)] = 6.53 m/s.
- A₂ = (π/4)(0.05)² = 1.963 × 10⁻³ m².
- Q = 0.98 × 1.963 × 10⁻³ × 6.53 = 0.0126 m³/s (12.6 L/s).
- If ΔP is read on a mercury-under-water manometer: h = ΔP/[(ρ_m − ρ)g] = 20 000/(12 600 × 9.81) = 0.162 m.

Orifice plate
A thin plate with a sharp-edged hole. The same equation applies (with the orifice area), but the jet keeps contracting downstream to a vena contracta and then expands turbulently, so:
- C_d is much lower, typically about 0.6 (approximate) for a sharp-edged orifice.
- Much of the pressure drop is not recovered, so the running (pumping) cost is higher.
- It is cheap, compact and easy to install or change, which is why it is so common.

Pitot tube
A tube facing into the flow brings fluid to rest at its tip (a stagnation point). The rise from static to stagnation pressure gives the local velocity:
u = √(2ΔP/ρ)
A pitot-static tube measures both pressures. Because it gives a point velocity, the flow rate needs a traverse across the pipe or a known velocity profile. Example: in air (ρ ≈ 1.2 kg/m³), ΔP = 200 Pa gives u = √(400/1.2) = 18.3 m/s.

Rotameter (variable-area meter)
A float rises in a tapered vertical tube until the drag and pressure forces balance its weight less buoyancy. The pressure drop stays roughly constant and the flow is read from the float height; calibration is specific to the fluid's density and viscosity.

Choosing a meter
- Venturi: low permanent loss, accurate, but long and expensive.
- Orifice: cheap and simple, high permanent loss.
- Pitot: point velocity, minimal obstruction, useful for gases and ducts.
- Rotameter: direct visual reading, small lines.

Exam tips: derive the venturi equation from Bernoulli and continuity rather than memorising it, keep β⁴ in the denominator, and remember the pitot result has no area term because it measures a velocity.

notes.h: Pipe flow: laminar and turbulent friction and pumping
notes.body:
Reynolds number
Re = ρuD/μ = uD/ν compares inertial to viscous forces. For flow in round pipes (approximate thresholds):
- Re below about 2000: laminar, smooth layers, parabolic velocity profile.
- Re roughly 2000–4000: transitional, unpredictable.
- Re above about 4000: turbulent, with eddies and a flatter mean profile.
Example: water (ρ = 1000 kg/m³, μ = 10⁻³ Pa s) at 1.5 m/s in a 50 mm pipe: Re = 1000 × 1.5 × 0.05/10⁻³ = 75 000, turbulent.

Wall shear stress and friction factors
A force balance on a length L of pipe gives ΔP(πD²/4) = τ_w(πDL), so ΔP = 4τ_wL/D. The wall stress is made dimensionless in different ways, so check which convention a formula sheet uses:
- Fanning friction factor: f = τ_w/(½ρu²); ΔP = 4f(L/D)(½ρu²).
- Darcy (Moody) friction factor: f_D = 4f; ΔP = f_D(L/D)(½ρu²).
- Coulson and Richardson's φ = R/(ρu²) = τ_w/(ρu²) = f/2, used in many UK chemical engineering courses; ΔP = 8φ(L/D)(½ρu²).

Laminar flow: Hagen–Poiseuille
For fully developed laminar flow, the profile is parabolic with u_max = 2u_mean and
ΔP = 32μLu/D² (u = mean velocity)
which corresponds to f = 16/Re (f_D = 64/Re, φ = 8/Re).
Example: oil (ρ = 900 kg/m³, μ = 0.1 Pa s) at 0.5 m/s in a 20 mm tube: Re = 90 (laminar), and over 10 m, ΔP = 32 × 0.1 × 10 × 0.5/0.02² = 40 kPa.
At fixed volumetric flow, u ∝ 1/D², so ΔP ∝ Q/D⁴: halving the diameter raises the laminar pressure drop sixteen-fold.

Turbulent flow
- In smooth pipes, the Blasius equation f = 0.079 Re^(−0.25) (Fanning) works for roughly 4000 < Re < 10⁵.
- For rough pipes, f depends on Re and the relative roughness e/D; read it from a Moody chart or use the Colebrook equation. At very high Re in rough pipes, f becomes nearly independent of Re.
Worked example (water, 1.5 m/s, 50 mm, 100 m smooth pipe):
- f = 0.079 × 75 000^(−0.25) = 0.00477 (f_D = 0.0191).
- ΔP = 4 × 0.00477 × (100/0.05) × ½ × 1000 × 1.5² = 43.0 kPa, a head loss of 4.38 m.
- Q = 1.5 × (π/4)(0.05)² = 2.95 × 10⁻³ m³/s; ideal power QΔP = 127 W; at 70% pump efficiency, about 181 W.

Minor losses
Fittings, valves, entrances and exits add losses written as K u²/(2g) of head, with K from tables. A pipe discharging into a large tank loses its full velocity head (K = 1).

Pumping
The pump head comes from the mechanical energy balance: h_pump = Δz + ΔP/(ρg) + Δ(u²/2g) + h_f (friction plus minor losses).

Exam tips: compute Re first to choose the friction law, state which friction factor convention you use, and quote head losses in metres as a sense check.

Fourier's law
Conduction is energy transfer through a material by molecular interaction (and by free electrons in metals), without bulk motion. In one dimension:
q = −k dT/dx
where q is heat flux (W/m²) and k thermal conductivity (W/m K). The minus sign says heat flows down the temperature gradient.

Typical conductivities near room temperature (approximate, W/m K)
- Copper ≈ 400; aluminium ≈ 200; carbon steel ≈ 45–50; stainless steel ≈ 15.
- Glass ≈ 1; brick ≈ 0.7; water ≈ 0.6.
- Mineral wool insulation ≈ 0.04; air ≈ 0.026.
Gases conduct poorly, which is why insulation works by trapping air in small pockets.

Plane wall at steady state
With constant k and no heat generation, the temperature profile is linear and
Q = kA(T₁ − T₂)/L.
Thermal resistance: R = L/(kA), so Q = ΔT/R, an analogy with Ohm's law (temperature difference as voltage, heat flow as current).

Resistances in series
For a composite wall with convection on both faces:
R_total = 1/(h_iA) + L₁/(k₁A) + L₂/(k₂A) + 1/(h_oA), and Q = (T_i − T_o)/R_total.

Worked example: insulated wall (per m²)
Inside air 20 °C (h_i = 10 W/m² K), 0.2 m brick (k = 0.7), 0.05 m mineral wool (k = 0.04), outside air 0 °C (h_o = 25 W/m² K).
- R = 0.100 + 0.286 + 1.250 + 0.040 = 1.676 m² K/W.
- q = 20/1.676 = 11.9 W/m².
- Inner wall surface: 20 − 11.9 × 0.1 = 18.8 °C; brick–insulation interface: 18.8 − 11.9 × 0.286 = 15.4 °C.
The largest resistance (the insulation) takes the largest share of the temperature drop.

Cylindrical walls (pipes)
Heat flows radially through an area that grows with r, so the profile is logarithmic. For length L:
R_cyl = ln(r₂/r₁)/(2πkL); convective resistance on the outside is 1/(h·2πr₂L).
Worked example: a steel pipe (r₁ = 50 mm, r₂ = 55 mm, k = 45) with 30 mm of insulation (k = 0.05, outer radius 85 mm), inner surface at 150 °C, air at 20 °C with h = 10 W/m² K. Per metre: R_steel = 0.0003, R_ins = 1.386, R_conv = 0.187 K m/W, so Q/L = 130/1.573 = 82.6 W/m. Without insulation, Q/L ≈ 449 W/m.

Critical radius of insulation
Adding insulation to a cylinder increases conduction resistance but also the outer area for convection. Heat loss is a maximum when the outer radius equals r_c = k/h (for a sphere, 2k/h). For the insulation above, r_c = 0.05/10 = 5 mm, much smaller than the pipe, so insulating it always helps. For thin wires, a thin coating can increase heat loss, which is useful for cooling electrical cables.

Unsteady conduction
Thermal diffusivity α = k/(ρc_p) (m²/s) controls how fast temperature changes spread; heat penetrates a distance of order √(αt) in time t.

Exam tips: draw the resistance network, compute each resistance with units, and check that the temperature drops add up to the overall difference.

Diffusion is the movement of a species relative to the mixture because of a concentration gradient, driven by random molecular motion. It is the mass transfer counterpart of conduction.

Fick's first law
For a binary mixture of A and B, the molar diffusion flux of A relative to the molar-average velocity is
J_A = −D_AB dC_A/dz
where D_AB is the binary diffusion coefficient (m²/s) and C_A the molar concentration (mol/m³). For an ideal gas C_A = p_A/(RT).

Typical diffusivities (approximate)
- Gases at 1 atm: of order 10⁻⁵ m²/s (water vapour in air at 25 °C ≈ 2.5–2.6 × 10⁻⁵).
- Liquids: of order 10⁻⁹ m²/s.
- Solids: much smaller and very variable.
Gas diffusivity rises with temperature and is inversely proportional to pressure. A useful time scale is t ≈ L²/D: diffusing 1 cm in a gas takes about 10 s, but diffusing 1 mm in a liquid takes about 1000 s, which is why liquid-phase processes rely on stirring and convection.

Total flux and bulk flow
The total molar flux relative to fixed coordinates is
N_A = J_A + x_A(N_A + N_B)
The second term is the bulk-flow contribution: if the mixture as a whole moves, it carries A with it.

Case 1: equimolar counter-diffusion (N_A = −N_B)
The bulk-flow term vanishes, and across a film of thickness L:
N_A = D_AB(C_A1 − C_A2)/L = D_AB(p_A1 − p_A2)/(RTL)
This approximates distillation, where roughly equal molar latent heats mean one mole condenses for each mole that evaporates.

Case 2: diffusion of A through stagnant B (N_B = 0)
Integrating with bulk flow gives
N_A = [D_AB P/(RTL)] ln[(P − p_A2)/(P − p_A1)] = D_AB P(p_A1 − p_A2)/(RTL p_BM)
where p_BM = (p_B2 − p_B1)/ln(p_B2/p_B1) is the log-mean partial pressure of B. Since P/p_BM > 1, the flux is larger than for equimolar counter-diffusion with the same driving force: the bulk flow helps. This models evaporation into air and gas absorption with an insoluble carrier gas.

Worked example: Stefan tube
Water evaporates at the bottom of a tube into dry air flowing across the top, 0.1 m above the liquid, at 25 °C and 101.325 kPa. Take vapour pressure ≈ 3.17 kPa and D ≈ 2.6 × 10⁻⁵ m²/s (both approximate).
- y_A1 = 3.17/101.325 = 0.0313; y_A2 = 0.
- N_A = [2.6 × 10⁻⁵ × 101 325/(8.314 × 298.15 × 0.1)] × ln[1/(1 − 0.0313)] = 3.38 × 10⁻⁴ mol/m² s.
- The equimolar formula would give 3.32 × 10⁻⁴ mol/m² s; the correction is small (about 1.6%) because the vapour is dilute. For concentrated systems the difference is large.

Exam tips: identify which flux condition applies (N_B = 0 or N_A = −N_B) before integrating, use consistent pressure units inside logarithms, and quote D values with their phase.

Convection is heat transfer between a surface and a moving fluid. It combines conduction in the fluid next to the wall with transport by the bulk motion of the fluid.

Newton's law of cooling
Q = hA(T_s − T_∞)
The heat transfer coefficient h (W/m² K) is not a material property: it depends on fluid properties, velocity, geometry and whether the flow is laminar or turbulent.

Typical h values (approximate ranges)
- Free convection, gases: 2–25 W/m² K; liquids: 50–1000.
- Forced convection, gases: 25–250; liquids: 100–20 000.
- Boiling and condensation: 2500–100 000.

Boundary layers
Near a wall, a velocity boundary layer forms where viscous effects matter, and a thermal boundary layer where the temperature changes from T_s to T_∞. Thin boundary layers give high h, which is why higher velocity and turbulence increase heat transfer.

Dimensionless groups
- Nusselt number Nu = hL/k_fluid: convective heat transfer relative to pure conduction across the fluid.
- Reynolds number Re = ρuL/μ: inertial vs viscous forces.
- Prandtl number Pr = c_pμ/k = ν/α: momentum diffusivity vs thermal diffusivity; about 0.7 for air and about 7 for water at room temperature (approximate).
- Grashof number Gr: buoyancy vs viscous forces, used for free convection.
Correlations have the form Nu = f(Re, Pr) for forced convection and Nu = f(Gr, Pr) for free convection.

Standard correlations for flow inside tubes
- Fully developed laminar flow: Nu = 3.66 for constant wall temperature; Nu = 4.36 for constant heat flux.
- Turbulent flow (Dittus–Boelter): Nu = 0.023 Re^0.8 Pr^n, with n = 0.4 when the fluid is being heated and 0.3 when it is being cooled; valid roughly for Re > 10⁴, 0.6 < Pr < 160 and long tubes (L/D > 10).

Worked example
Water at about 30 °C flows at 1 m/s in a 25 mm tube and is being heated. Approximate properties: ρ = 996 kg/m³, μ = 7.98 × 10⁻⁴ Pa s, k = 0.615 W/m K, Pr = 5.42.
- Re = 996 × 1 × 0.025/7.98 × 10⁻⁴ = 31 200 (turbulent).
- Nu = 0.023 × 31 200^0.8 × 5.42^0.4 = 178.
- h = Nu k/D = 178 × 0.615/0.025 ≈ 4400 W/m² K.

Overall heat transfer coefficient
For a thin plane wall between two fluids, resistances add:
1/U = 1/h_i + L/k_w + 1/h_o (+ fouling resistances).
Example: h_i = 5000, h_o = 1000 W/m² K, wall negligible: U = 1/(0.0002 + 0.001) = 833 W/m² K. The smaller coefficient controls, so improving it gives the biggest gain. For thick tubes, base U on a stated area (inner or outer).

Heat exchangers
With temperatures changing along the exchanger, Q = UAΔT_lm, where ΔT_lm = (ΔT₁ − ΔT₂)/ln(ΔT₁/ΔT₂), using the terminal temperature differences. For a counter-current exchanger, hot 150 → 90 °C and cold 30 → 70 °C: ΔT₁ = 80 K, ΔT₂ = 60 K, ΔT_lm = 69.5 K.

Exam tips: check Re and Pr are inside a correlation's range, use the fluid's k (not the wall's) in Nu, and identify the controlling resistance.

notes.h: Convective mass transfer and heat–mass transfer analogies
notes.body:
Mass transfer coefficients
When a fluid flows past a surface that releases or absorbs species A, the flux is written by analogy with Newton's law of cooling:
N_A = k_c(C_As − C_A∞)
where k_c (m/s) is the mass transfer coefficient. Like h, it depends on flow, geometry and properties. Coefficients can also be based on partial pressure (k_G) or mole fraction (k_y), so check units: k_y = k_c C for a gas with total molar concentration C.

Dimensionless groups for mass transfer
- Sherwood number Sh = k_cL/D_AB: the mass transfer analogue of Nu.
- Schmidt number Sc = μ/(ρD_AB) = ν/D_AB: the analogue of Pr. For gases Sc is typically about 0.5–2 (water vapour in air ≈ 0.6); for liquids it is typically hundreds to thousands (approximate).
- Lewis number Le = α/D_AB = Sc/Pr: compares heat and mass diffusivities; for water vapour in air it is close to 1 (about 0.85, approximate).

The analogy
Because the equations for convective heat and mass transfer have the same form, a heat transfer correlation Nu = C Re^m Pr^n can be converted to a mass transfer one by replacing Nu with Sh and Pr with Sc: Sh = C Re^m Sc^n, provided geometry, flow and boundary conditions match and mass transfer rates are low.
Examples:
- Sphere in a stagnant fluid: Nu = 2, so Sh = 2.
- Sphere in flowing fluid (Ranz–Marshall): Nu = 2 + 0.6 Re^½ Pr^⅓ ↔ Sh = 2 + 0.6 Re^½ Sc^⅓.
- Turbulent flow in tubes: Sh = 0.023 Re^0.83 Sc^⅓, usually attributed to Linton and Sherwood (1950), whose data came from solids dissolving into liquids at high Schmidt numbers. The earlier Gilliland–Sherwood correlation (1934), from evaporation of liquids into air in wetted-wall columns (Sc roughly 0.6–2.5), has the same Re exponent but Sc^0.44. Both have the same form as Dittus–Boelter.

Reynolds and Chilton–Colburn analogies
Momentum, heat and mass are transported by the same eddies in turbulent flow.
- Reynolds analogy (valid for Pr = Sc = 1): St = St_m = f/2, with St = h/(ρc_pu) and St_m = k_c/u (f is the Fanning friction factor).
- Chilton–Colburn: j_H = St Pr^⅔ = f/2 and j_D = St_m Sc^⅔ = f/2, extending the result to Pr and Sc away from 1 (for flows without form drag).
- Setting j_H = j_D gives h/k_c = ρc_p Le^⅔, which lets you estimate a mass transfer coefficient from a heat transfer measurement.

Worked example
Air at 25 °C flows over a wet surface with h = 20 W/m² K. Take ρ ≈ 1.18 kg/m³, c_p ≈ 1007 J/kg K and Le ≈ 0.85 (approximate).
- ρc_p = 1188 J/m³ K; Le^⅔ = 0.897.
- k_c = 20/(1188 × 0.897) = 0.0188 m/s.
- If the surface is held at 25 °C and the air is dry, C_As = p_sat/(RT) = 3170/(8.314 × 298.15) = 1.28 mol/m³, so N_A = 0.0188 × 1.28 = 0.024 mol/m² s (about 0.43 g/m² s).
In reality evaporation cools the surface, lowering p_sat until heat gained by convection balances the latent heat removed: this is the principle of the wet-bulb thermometer.

Exam tips: write the analogy explicitly (which group maps to which), keep Sc and Pr exponents consistent, and state that the analogy assumes low mass transfer rates and similar boundary conditions.

ΔP = (ρ_m − ρ)gh, with ρ_m the manometer fluid and ρ the fluid above it.

Energy per unit weight of fluid, in metres: pressure head P/(ρg), velocity head u²/(2g), elevation head z.

cards.f: Mechanical energy balance with pump and friction
cards.b: P₁/ρg + u₁²/2g + z₁ + h_pump = P₂/ρg + u₂²/2g + z₂ + h_f.
ρgQh_pump/η, where h_pump is the head added and η the pump efficiency.
Corrects u²/2 when using mean velocity: about 2 for laminar pipe flow, about 1 for turbulent.
Q = C_d A₂ √[2ΔP/(ρ(1 − β⁴))], β = d_throat/d_pipe; from Bernoulli plus continuity.
Venturi ≈ 0.95–0.99; sharp-edged orifice ≈ 0.6.
The narrowest section of the jet just downstream of an orifice, where the velocity is highest and pressure lowest.
u = √(2ΔP/ρ), ΔP = stagnation minus static pressure; it gives a local (point) velocity.

cards.f: Why does an orifice plate have a high permanent pressure loss?
cards.b: The jet expands abruptly and turbulently after the vena contracta, dissipating most of the kinetic energy instead of recovering it as pressure.
Variable-area meter: a float rises in a tapered tube until forces balance; nearly constant pressure drop; calibration depends on fluid properties.
Re = ρuD/μ: ratio of inertial to viscous forces. In pipes, laminar below about 2000, turbulent above about 4000 (approx.).
ΔP = 32μLu/D² for fully developed laminar flow in a round pipe (u = mean velocity).
Fanning f = 16/Re; Darcy f_D = 64/Re; Coulson & Richardson φ = 8/Re.
Darcy f_D = 4 × Fanning f = 8 × φ (φ = R/ρu²). Always check which a chart or formula uses.
Fanning f = 0.079 Re^(−0.25) for turbulent flow in smooth pipes, roughly 4000 < Re < 10⁵.

cards.f: Laminar ΔP when D is halved at fixed Q
cards.b: Rises 16-fold, since ΔP ∝ Q/D⁴.
Head loss K u²/(2g) for a valve, bend, entrance or exit; an exit into a large tank has K ≈ 1.

cards.f: Laminar velocity profile in a pipe
cards.b: Parabolic: u(r) = u_max(1 − r²/R²), with u_max = 2 × mean velocity.
q = −k dT/dx: conductive heat flux is proportional to the temperature gradient, flowing from hot to cold.
R = L/(kA); Q = ΔT/R.
R = ln(r₂/r₁)/(2πkL).
r_c = k/h; heat loss is maximum when the outer radius equals r_c. For a sphere r_c = 2k/h.
Copper ≈ 400 > carbon steel ≈ 45–50 > glass ≈ 1 > water ≈ 0.6 > mineral wool ≈ 0.04 > air ≈ 0.026 W/m K.
α = k/(ρc_p), m²/s; governs transient conduction (penetration depth ~ √(αt)).

cards.f: Temperature profile, steady plane wall, constant k
cards.b: Linear; in a cylindrical wall it is logarithmic in r.
J_A = −D_AB dC_A/dz: diffusive molar flux of A is proportional to its concentration gradient.
Gases at 1 atm ~10⁻⁵ m²/s; liquids ~10⁻⁹ m²/s.
N_A = J_A + x_A(N_A + N_B): diffusion plus bulk-flow contribution.
N_A = −N_B; N_A = D(C_A1 − C_A2)/L. A good model for distillation.
N_A = [DP/(RTL)] ln[(P − p_A2)/(P − p_A1)] = DP(p_A1 − p_A2)/(RTL p_BM). Models evaporation into air and absorption from an inert gas.
p_BM = (p_B2 − p_B1)/ln(p_B2/p_B1).
t ~ L²/D: about 10 s for 1 cm in a gas, about 1000 s for 1 mm in a liquid.
Q = hA(T_s − T_∞); h depends on flow, geometry and fluid properties, not just the material.
Nu = hL/k (k of the fluid): ratio of convective to conductive heat transfer across the fluid layer.
Pr = c_pμ/k = ν/α; about 0.7 for air and about 7 for water at room temperature (approx.).
Nu = 0.023 Re^0.8 Pr^n (n = 0.4 heating the fluid, 0.3 cooling); turbulent tube flow, Re > 10⁴, 0.6 < Pr < 160.

cards.f: Laminar fully developed Nu in a tube
cards.b: 3.66 at constant wall temperature; 4.36 at constant heat flux.
1/U = 1/h_i + L/k_w + 1/h_o (+ fouling); the largest resistance (smallest h) controls.
ΔT_lm = (ΔT₁ − ΔT₂)/ln(ΔT₁/ΔT₂) from the two terminal differences; Q = UAΔT_lm.
About 2500–100 000 W/m² K, far above forced convection of gases (25–250).
k_c in N_A = k_c(C_As − C_A∞), units m/s; depends on flow, geometry and properties.
Sh = k_cL/D_AB, the mass transfer analogue of the Nusselt number.
Sc = ν/D_AB = μ/(ρD_AB): momentum vs mass diffusivity; ~0.6 for water vapour in air, hundreds to thousands in liquids (approx.).
Le = α/D_AB = Sc/Pr; about 0.85 for water vapour in air (approx.).
j_H = St Pr^⅔ = f/2 and j_D = St_m Sc^⅔ = f/2 (f = Fanning friction factor).

cards.f: Converting a heat transfer correlation to mass transfer
cards.b: Replace Nu by Sh and Pr by Sc, keeping the same constants and exponents.

cards.f: Sh for a sphere in a stagnant fluid
cards.b: Sh = 2 (analogue of Nu = 2 for pure conduction from a sphere).
h/k_c = ρc_p Le^⅔ (from j_H = j_D).

questions.q: What is the gauge pressure at the bottom of a 5 m deep open tank of oil with density 850 kg/m³ (g = 9.81 m/s²)?
questions.why: P = ρgh = 850 × 9.81 × 5 = 41.7 kPa gauge. 49.1 kPa uses the density of water instead of the oil. 4.25 kPa leaves out g, giving ρh in the wrong units. 143.0 kPa adds atmospheric pressure, which is the absolute rather than the gauge value.

questions.q: What are the SI units of dynamic viscosity?
questions.why: From τ = μ du/dy, μ = Pa ÷ (1/s) = Pa s. m²/s is the unit of kinematic viscosity, μ/ρ. Pa/s would be a rate of change of pressure. N/m is the unit of surface tension.

questions.q: An open tank contains 3 m of water (ρ = 1000 kg/m³) with a 2 m layer of oil (ρ = 850 kg/m³) floating on top. Find the gauge and absolute pressures at the base (atmosphere 101.3 kPa, g = 9.81 m/s²).
markScheme: Pressure at the oil–water interface = 850 × 9.81 × 2 = 16.7 kPa gauge (1 mark)
questions.modelAnswer: Start at the free surface (0 gauge). Through the oil: ΔP = 850 × 9.81 × 2 = 16.7 kPa, so the interface is at 16.7 kPa gauge. Through the water: ΔP = 1000 × 9.81 × 3 = 29.4 kPa. Base pressure = 16.7 + 29.4 = 46.1 kPa gauge, or 46.1 + 101.3 = 147.4 kPa absolute.

questions.q: Water flows at 2 m/s in a pipe whose diameter then halves. What is the mean velocity in the narrower section?
questions.why: Area scales with d², so halving d quarters the area and continuity gives u = 2 × 4 = 8 m/s. 4 m/s assumes velocity scales with 1/d rather than 1/d². 0.5 m/s inverts the area ratio, as if the fluid slowed down. 2 m/s assumes velocity is unchanged, which would violate conservation of mass.

questions.q: A large open tank has a small hole 5 m below the water surface. Neglecting losses, what is the jet velocity?
questions.why: Torricelli: u = √(2gh) = √(2 × 9.81 × 5) = 9.90 m/s. 98.1 is 2gh without the square root (and its units are m²/s², not a velocity). 7.00 m/s is √(gh), which drops the factor of 2 from ½u². 49.1 is gh with neither the 2 nor the square root.

questions.q: Water (ρ = 1000 kg/m³) flows at 2.0 m/s through a horizontal 100 mm diameter pipe that contracts smoothly to 50 mm. Neglecting friction, find the volumetric flow, the velocity in the contraction and the pressure drop between the two sections.
markScheme: Bernoulli between the sections with z₁ = z₂ (1 mark)
questions.modelAnswer: Q = A₁u₁ = (π/4)(0.10)² × 2.0 = 0.0157 m³/s. Continuity: u₂ = u₁(d₁/d₂)² = 2.0 × 4 = 8.0 m/s. Bernoulli along the axis, horizontal so z cancels: P₁ − P₂ = ½ρ(u₂² − u₁²) = 0.5 × 1000 × (64 − 4) = 30 000 Pa = 30 kPa. The pressure falls where the velocity rises.

questions.q: A pitot-static tube in an air duct (ρ = 1.2 kg/m³) shows a difference of 200 Pa between stagnation and static pressure. What is the air velocity at the tip?
questions.why: u = √(2ΔP/ρ) = √(400/1.2) = 18.3 m/s. 0.63 m/s uses the density of water (1000 kg/m³) instead of air. 12.9 m/s leaves out the factor of 2, using √(ΔP/ρ). 333 m/s is 2ΔP/ρ without the square root, which is a velocity squared.

questions.q: Why is the discharge coefficient of a sharp-edged orifice plate (about 0.6) much lower than that of a venturi meter (about 0.98)?
options: Orifice plates are always installed vertically, so gravity reduces the flow
The jet contracts to a vena contracta smaller than the hole, and the flow separates with large losses
Orifice plates can only be used for gases, whose density changes
The orifice equation leaves out the β⁴ term
questions.why: Using the hole area overstates the actual jet area, because the jet keeps contracting downstream of the plate, and the abrupt geometry causes separation and dissipation; both lower the real flow for a given ΔP. Orifice plates are widely used for liquids as well as gases. The standard orifice equation has the same β⁴ form as the venturi. Orifice plates can be installed in pipes of any orientation; gravity is not the reason for the low coefficient.

questions.q: A venturi meter with a 100 mm inlet and a 50 mm throat carries water (ρ = 1000 kg/m³). A mercury-under-water manometer (ρ_m = 13 600 kg/m³) connected between inlet and throat reads 162 mm. Taking C_d = 0.98, find the pressure difference and the flow rate.
markScheme: Bernoulli and continuity combined to give u₂ = √[2ΔP/(ρ(1 − β⁴))] with β = 0.5 (1 mark)
questions.modelAnswer: ΔP = (13 600 − 1000) × 9.81 × 0.162 = 2.00 × 10⁴ Pa. Bernoulli between inlet and throat (horizontal) gives P₁ − P₂ = ½ρ(u₂² − u₁²), and continuity gives u₁ = u₂β² with β = 0.5, so u₂ = √[2ΔP/(ρ(1 − β⁴))] = √[40 000/(1000 × 0.9375)] = 6.53 m/s. Throat area = (π/4)(0.05)² = 1.963 × 10⁻³ m². Q = 0.98 × 1.963 × 10⁻³ × 6.53 = 0.0126 m³/s (12.6 L/s).

questions.q: Laminar flow passes through a pipe at a fixed volumetric flow rate. If the pipe diameter is halved, by what factor does the pressure drop per unit length change?
questions.why: ΔP = 32μLu/D² and at fixed Q the mean velocity u ∝ 1/D², so ΔP ∝ 1/D⁴ and halving D multiplies it by 16. A factor of 4 holds the velocity constant rather than the flow rate. A factor of 2 treats the pressure drop as inversely proportional to diameter only. 16 times smaller has the right magnitude but the wrong direction: a narrower pipe always needs more pressure for the same flow.

questions.q: Water (ρ = 1000 kg/m³, μ = 1.0 × 10⁻³ Pa s) flows at 2 m/s in a 25 mm pipe. What is the Reynolds number and flow regime?
questions.why: Re = 1000 × 2 × 0.025/0.001 = 5.0 × 10⁴, well above about 4000, so turbulent. 50 results from entering the viscosity as 1 (its value in mPa s) instead of 10⁻³ Pa s. 5.0 × 10⁷ uses the diameter in millimetres instead of metres. 5.0 × 10⁴ is the right number, but a value that high is not laminar in a pipe.

questions.q: Water (ρ = 1000 kg/m³, μ = 1.0 × 10⁻³ Pa s) flows at 1.5 m/s through 100 m of smooth 50 mm bore pipe. Using the Blasius equation f = 0.079 Re^(−0.25) (Fanning), find the frictional pressure drop, the head loss and the power needed to overcome friction with a 70% efficient pump.
markScheme: Re = 75 000, turbulent so Blasius applies (1 mark)

questions.q: A plane wall 0.1 m thick with k = 1.0 W/m K and area 2 m² has faces at 70 °C and 20 °C. What is the steady heat flow?
questions.why: Q = kAΔT/L = 1.0 × 2 × 50/0.1 = 1000 W. 500 W is the heat flux in W/m², which leaves out the area. 10 W multiplies by the thickness instead of dividing by it. 250 W divides by the area instead of multiplying.

questions.q: Insulation with k = 0.05 W/m K is applied to a long cylinder in air with an outside heat transfer coefficient h = 10 W/m² K. What is the critical radius of insulation?
options: There is no critical radius: adding insulation always reduces heat loss
questions.why: For a cylinder, r_c = k/h = 0.05/10 = 0.005 m = 5 mm. 10 mm is 2k/h, the critical radius for a sphere, not a cylinder. 500 mm comes from multiplying k by h instead of dividing. The claim that there is no critical radius is wrong: below r_c, adding insulation increases the outer surface area for convection faster than it adds conduction resistance, so heat loss rises.

questions.q: A wall consists of 0.2 m of brick (k = 0.7 W/m K) and 0.05 m of insulation (k = 0.04 W/m K). Inside air is at 20 °C with h = 10 W/m² K; outside air is at 0 °C with h = 25 W/m² K. Find the heat loss per m² and the temperature at the brick–insulation interface.
markScheme: Series resistances per m²: 0.100, 0.286, 1.250 and 0.040 m² K/W (2 marks)
Total 1.676 m² K/W; q = 20/1.676 = 11.9 W/m² (1 mark)
questions.modelAnswer: Per m², resistances in series: inside film 1/10 = 0.100; brick 0.2/0.7 = 0.286; insulation 0.05/0.04 = 1.250; outside film 1/25 = 0.040; total 1.676 m² K/W. q = (20 − 0)/1.676 = 11.9 W/m². Interface temperature = 20 − 11.9 × (0.100 + 0.286) = 20 − 4.6 = 15.4 °C. Most of the 20 K drop (about 15 K) occurs across the insulation, which has the largest resistance.

questions.q: Which value is a typical order of magnitude for the diffusion coefficient of a small solute molecule in a liquid at room temperature?
questions.why: Small solutes in liquids such as water typically have D around 10⁻⁹ m²/s. 10⁻⁵ m²/s is typical of gases at atmospheric pressure, where molecules are far apart. 10⁻² m²/s is far larger than any molecular diffusivity at ordinary conditions. 10⁻¹⁴ m²/s is in the range of slow diffusion in solids.

questions.q: For the same partial-pressure driving force, film thickness and diffusivity, how does the flux of A diffusing through stagnant B compare with equimolar counter-diffusion?
options: It is identical, because Fick's law is the same
It is zero, because B is not moving
It is larger by a factor P/p_BM, because bulk flow adds to diffusion
It is smaller by a factor P/p_BM, because stagnant B resists the flow of A
questions.why: With N_B = 0 the bulk flow carries A in the same direction as diffusion, giving N_A = DP Δp_A/(RTL p_BM), larger by P/p_BM than the equimolar result. The flux is not reduced: B diffuses back towards the interface, but its diffusion is cancelled by bulk flow, leaving B with zero net flux, not a resistance that slows A. The fluxes are not identical because the bulk-flow term differs between the two cases. A non-moving B does not stop A diffusing; it only sets N_B = 0.

questions.q: Water evaporates from the bottom of a narrow tube into dry air blowing across the top, 0.10 m above the liquid surface, at 25 °C and 101.325 kPa. Taking the vapour pressure of water as 3.17 kPa and D = 2.6 × 10⁻⁵ m²/s, calculate the molar flux of water vapour and state the key assumption.
markScheme: Model as diffusion of A through stagnant B (air insoluble in water, N_B = 0) at steady state (1 mark)
y_A1 = 0.0313 at the liquid surface, y_A2 = 0 at the top (1 mark)
questions.modelAnswer: Air does not dissolve in water, so at steady state N_air = 0 and water vapour diffuses through stagnant air (the level drop is slow enough to treat L as constant). At the surface the gas is saturated: y_A1 = 3.17/101.325 = 0.0313; at the top y_A2 = 0. N_A = [DP/(RTL)] ln[(1 − y_A2)/(1 − y_A1)]. DP/(RTL) = 2.6 × 10⁻⁵ × 101 325/(8.314 × 298.15 × 0.10) = 0.0106 mol/m² s. ln(1/0.9687) = 0.0318. N_A = 0.0106 × 0.0318 = 3.4 × 10⁻⁴ mol/m² s.

questions.q: The film coefficients on either side of a thin metal wall are 5000 W/m² K and 1000 W/m² K. Neglecting the wall and fouling, what is the overall heat transfer coefficient?
questions.why: The resistances add in series: 1/U = 1/5000 + 1/1000 = 0.0012, so U = 833 W/m² K. 6000 adds the coefficients themselves, which would treat the films as parallel paths. 3000 is the arithmetic mean of the coefficients, which has no physical basis. 1000 assumes the smaller coefficient alone sets U; it controls, but the other film still adds resistance, so U must be lower than 1000.

questions.q: What physical ratio does the Prandtl number represent?
options: Convective to conductive heat transfer at a surface
questions.why: Pr = ν/α compares how fast momentum and heat diffuse, so it relates the thicknesses of velocity and thermal boundary layers. The inertial to viscous ratio is the Reynolds number. Convective to conductive heat transfer at a surface is the Nusselt number. Buoyancy to viscous forces is the Grashof number.

questions.q: Water is heated while flowing at 1.0 m/s through a 25 mm bore tube. Take ρ = 996 kg/m³, μ = 7.98 × 10⁻⁴ Pa s, k = 0.615 W/m K and Pr = 5.42. Use the Dittus–Boelter equation to estimate the tube-side heat transfer coefficient, and justify using it.
markScheme: Pr within range, n = 0.4 chosen because the fluid is heated (1 mark)
questions.modelAnswer: Re = ρuD/μ = 996 × 1.0 × 0.025/7.98 × 10⁻⁴ = 31 200, fully turbulent and above 10⁴; Pr = 5.42 lies within about 0.6–160, so Dittus–Boelter applies (assuming the tube is long, L/D > 10). The fluid is being heated, so n = 0.4. Nu = 0.023 × 31 200^0.8 × 5.42^0.4 = 0.023 × 3940 × 1.97 ≈ 178. h = Nu k/D = 178 × 0.615/0.025 ≈ 4380 W/m² K.

questions.q: Which ratio defines the Schmidt number?
questions.why: Sc = ν/D_AB compares momentum and mass diffusion. Thermal diffusivity over mass diffusivity is the Lewis number. Kinematic viscosity over thermal diffusivity is the Prandtl number. k_cL/D_AB is the Sherwood number, a dimensionless mass transfer coefficient.

questions.q: What is the Sherwood number for steady mass transfer from a small sphere into a large, completely stagnant fluid (diameter as the length scale)?
questions.why: Pure diffusion outward from a sphere into an infinite medium gives k_cD/D_AB = 2, the analogue of Nu = 2 for conduction. Zero would mean no transfer at all, but diffusion still carries mass away without flow. A value of 1 comes from treating the surrounding fluid as a flat film one diameter thick, which is not the spherical solution. 3.66 is the laminar Nusselt number for fully developed flow in a tube at constant wall temperature, a different geometry.

questions.q: Air at 25 °C flows over a wet surface; the heat transfer coefficient is 20 W/m² K. Taking ρ = 1.18 kg/m³, c_p = 1007 J/kg K and Le = 0.85, use the Chilton–Colburn analogy to estimate the mass transfer coefficient k_c. Then find the evaporation flux if the surface is at 25 °C (p_sat = 3.17 kPa) and the air is dry.
markScheme: Analogy j_H = j_D gives h/k_c = ρc_p Le^⅔ (1 mark)
questions.modelAnswer: Equating j_H = St Pr^⅔ and j_D = St_m Sc^⅔ gives h/k_c = ρc_p(Sc/Pr)^⅔ = ρc_p Le^⅔. ρc_p = 1.18 × 1007 = 1188 J/m³ K and 0.85^⅔ = 0.897, so k_c = 20/(1188 × 0.897) = 0.0188 m/s. At the surface C_As = 3170/(8.314 × 298.15) = 1.28 mol/m³; dry air gives C_A∞ = 0. N_A = 0.0188 × 1.28 = 0.024 mol/m² s (about 4.3 × 10⁻⁴ kg/m² s).

questions.q:
Water (ρ = 1000 kg/m³, μ = 1.0 × 10⁻³ Pa s) is pumped at 1.5 m/s from an open tank through 100 m of smooth 50 mm bore pipe into a second open tank whose free surface is 15 m higher. The pipe discharges below the surface of the upper tank. Neglect all minor losses except the exit loss.
(a) Calculate the Reynolds number and justify the friction law you use. [3]
(b) Using the Blasius equation (Fanning f = 0.079 Re^(−0.25)), find the frictional head loss. [5]
(c) Apply the mechanical energy balance between the two free surfaces to find the pump head, and find the shaft power for a pump efficiency of 70%. [7]
(d) Estimate the new friction head and pump head if the flow rate is doubled, and comment on your answer. [5]
markScheme: Re = 75 000: turbulent, inside Blasius range for smooth pipes (3 marks)
Energy balance between free surfaces: P and u terms cancel (atmospheric, negligible velocity); h_pump = Δz + h_f + exit loss u²/2g (3 marks)
Exit loss = 0.115 m; h_pump ≈ 19.5 m (2 marks)
Q = 2.95 × 10⁻³ m³/s; shaft power = ρgQh/η ≈ 0.80 kW (2 marks)
Doubled flow: Re = 1.5 × 10⁵ (slightly outside Blasius range), h_f ∝ u^1.75, so h_f ≈ 14.7 m and h_pump ≈ 30.2 m (3 marks)
Comment: friction head rises about 3.4 times, power more than triple; Blasius extrapolated so estimate approximate (2 marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Re = ρuD/μ = 1000 × 1.5 × 0.05/1.0 × 10⁻³ = 75 000. This is well above about 4000, so the flow is turbulent; the pipe is smooth and Re is below 10⁵, inside the range of the Blasius equation.

(b) f = 0.079 × 75 000^(−0.25) = 0.079/16.55 = 0.00477 (Darcy f_D = 0.0191).
ΔP_f = 4f(L/D)(½ρu²) = 4 × 0.00477 × (100/0.05) × (0.5 × 1000 × 1.5²) = 0.0191 × 2000 × 1125 = 4.30 × 10⁴ Pa.
h_f = ΔP_f/(ρg) = 43 000/9810 = 4.38 m.

(c) Mechanical energy balance from the lower free surface (1) to the upper free surface (2): P₁ = P₂ = atmospheric and u₁ ≈ u₂ ≈ 0 for large tanks, so
h_pump = (z₂ − z₁) + h_f + h_exit.
The exit loss when the pipe discharges into the tank is one velocity head: u²/(2g) = 1.5²/(2 × 9.81) = 0.115 m.
h_pump = 15 + 4.38 + 0.115 = 19.5 m.
Q = 1.5 × (π/4)(0.05)² = 2.95 × 10⁻³ m³/s.
Power to the fluid = ρgQh = 1000 × 9.81 × 2.95 × 10⁻³ × 19.5 = 563 W; shaft power = 563/0.70 ≈ 805 W (about 0.80 kW).

(d) Doubling Q doubles u to 3.0 m/s and Re to 1.5 × 10⁵. With Blasius, f ∝ Re^(−0.25), so ΔP ∝ f u² ∝ u^1.75: h_f = 4.38 × 2^1.75 = 4.38 × 3.36 = 14.7 m. Exit loss = 3²/(2 × 9.81) = 0.46 m. h_pump = 15 + 14.7 + 0.46 = 30.2 m.
Comment: the static lift is unchanged, but friction head rises about 3.4 times, so the pump head rises from about 19.5 m to about 30 m; with twice the flow the hydraulic power rises roughly threefold (about 2 × 30.2/19.5 ≈ 3.1 times). Re = 1.5 × 10⁵ is just outside the usual Blasius range, so the estimate is approximate; a Moody chart or the Colebrook equation would be better. Larger pipes reduce running costs at higher capital cost, the classic optimum pipe diameter trade-off.

questions.q:
A steel steam pipe (inner radius 50 mm, outer radius 55 mm, k = 45 W/m K) has its inner surface at 150 °C. It is lagged with 30 mm of insulation (k = 0.05 W/m K). The surrounding air is at 20 °C with an outside heat transfer coefficient of 10 W/m² K. Neglect radiation.
(a) Draw the thermal resistance network and calculate each resistance per metre of pipe. [6]
(b) Find the heat loss per metre and the outer surface temperature of the insulation. [5]
(c) Find the heat loss per metre from the bare pipe and the percentage saving from lagging. [4]
(d) Explain the concept of a critical radius of insulation and whether it matters here. [5]
markScheme: Network: steel conduction, insulation conduction and outside convection in series (2 marks)
Critical radius r_c = k/h = 5 mm; explanation of competing conduction and convection resistances; pipe radius 55 mm > r_c so insulation always reduces loss here (5 marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Heat flows from the inner pipe surface (150 °C) through the steel, then the insulation, then by convection to the air (20 °C): three resistances in series. Per metre length:
R_steel = ln(r₂/r₁)/(2πk) = ln(55/50)/(2π × 45) = 0.0953/282.7 = 3.4 × 10⁻⁴ K m/W.
R_ins = ln(85/55)/(2π × 0.05) = 0.4353/0.3142 = 1.386 K m/W.
R_conv = 1/(h × 2πr₃) = 1/(10 × 2π × 0.085) = 0.187 K m/W.
Total = 1.573 K m/W.

(b) Q/L = (150 − 20)/1.573 = 82.6 W/m.
Outer insulation surface: T₃ = 20 + (Q/L)R_conv = 20 + 82.6 × 0.187 = 35.5 °C. (The steel–insulation interface is at 150 − 82.6 × 0.00034 ≈ 150.0 °C: the steel resistance is negligible.)

(c) Bare pipe: R = 3.4 × 10⁻⁴ + 1/(10 × 2π × 0.055) = 3.4 × 10⁻⁴ + 0.289 = 0.290 K m/W, giving Q/L = 130/0.290 ≈ 449 W/m. Lagging cuts the loss from about 449 to 82.6 W/m, a saving of (449 − 82.6)/449 ≈ 82%. (Radiation from the hot bare surface would add further loss in practice, so the real saving is larger.)

(d) For a cylinder, adding insulation increases the conduction resistance ln(r/r₂)/(2πk), but it also increases the outer surface area, so the convection resistance 1/(2πrh) falls. The total resistance has a minimum (heat loss a maximum) at r = r_c = k/h. Below r_c, adding a little insulation actually increases heat loss; above r_c, more insulation always reduces it. Here r_c = 0.05/10 = 0.005 m = 5 mm. The bare pipe radius (55 mm) is already well above r_c, so any thickness of this insulation reduces heat loss. The effect matters for small diameters such as electrical wires, where a thin insulating coating can increase cooling.
